{{Short description|Phenomenon observed in the study of Artificial Neural Networks}}
{{Orphan|date=December 2024}}

The '''frequency principle/spectral bias''' is a phenomenon observed in the study of [[Artificial neural network|artificial neural networks (ANNs)]], specifically [[Deep learning#Deep neural networks|deep neural networks (DNNs)]]. It describes the tendency of deep neural networks to fit target functions from low to high frequencies during the training process.

This phenomenon is referred to as the frequency principle (F-Principle) by Zhi-Qin John Xu et al.<ref name="ipsum">{{Cite book| publisher = Springer International Publishing| isbn = 978-3-030-36707-7 | volume = 11953| pages = 264–274| editor = Tom Gedeon |editor2=Kok Wai Wong |editor3=Minho Lee | last1 = Xu| first1 = Zhi-Qin John| last2 = Zhang| first2 = Yaoyu| last3 = Xiao| first3 = Yanyang| title = Neural Information Processing| chapter = Training Behavior of Deep Neural Network in Frequency Domain| location = Cham| date = 2019| doi = 10.1007/978-3-030-36708-4_22 | arxiv = 1807.01251 | s2cid = 49562099 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.4208/cicp.OA-2020-0085| issn = 1815-2406| volume = 28| issue = 5| pages = 1746–1767| last1 = Xu| first1 = Zhi-Qin John| last2 = Zhang| first2 = Yaoyu| last3 = Luo| first3 = Tao| last4 = Xiao| first4 = Yanyang| last5 = Ma| first5 = Zheng| title = Frequency Principle: Fourier Analysis Sheds Light on Deep Neural Networks| journal = Communications in Computational Physics| date = 2020| arxiv = 1901.06523| bibcode = 2020CCoPh..28.1746X| s2cid = 58981616}}</ref> or spectral bias by Nasim Rahaman et al.<ref>{{Cite conference| publisher = PMLR| conference = International Conference on Machine Learning| pages = 5301–5310| last1 = Rahaman| first1 = Nasim| last2 = Baratin| first2 = Aristide| last3 = Arpit| first3 = Devansh| last4 = Draxler| first4 = Felix| last5 = Lin| first5 = Min| last6 = Hamprecht| first6 = Fred| last7 = Bengio| first7 = Yoshua| last8 = Courville| first8 = Aaron| title = On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks| book-title = Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning| accessdate = 2023-07-14| date = 2019-05-24| url = https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/rahaman19a.html}}</ref> The F-Principle can be robustly observed in DNNs, regardless of [[Neural tangent kernel#Overparametrization, interpolation, and generalization|overparametrization]]. A key mechanism of the F-Principle is that the regularity of the [[activation function]] translates into the decay rate of the [[loss function]] in the [[frequency domain]].

The discovery of the frequency principle has inspired the design of DNNs that can quickly learn high-frequency functions. This has applications in [[Computational science|scientific computing]], image classification, and [[point cloud]] fitting problems. Furthermore, it provides a means to comprehend phenomena in practical applications and has inspired numerous studies on deep learning from the frequency perspective.<ref name="ofp">{{cite arXiv| eprint = 2201.07395| last1 = Xu| first1 = Zhi-Qin John| last2 = Zhang| first2 = Yaoyu| last3 = Luo| first3 = Tao| title = Overview frequency principle/spectral bias in deep learning| date = 2022-10-18| class = cs.LG}}</ref>

==Main results (informal)==
===Experimental results===
[[File:F-Principle one dim.gif|thumb|Fig 1: This image illustrates the frequency principle in one-dimension. The abscissa represents the frequency and the ordinate represents the amplitude to the corresponding frequency. The red dash line is the DFT of the one-dimension target function. The blue solid line is the DFT of the DNNs output.]]

In one-dimensional problems, the [[Discrete Fourier transform|Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)]] of the target function and the output of DNNs can be obtained, and we can observe from Fig.1 that the blue line fits the low-frequency faster than the high-frequency.

[[File:Frequency experiment two dimension.png|thumb|Fig 2: The picture illustrates the frequency in the two-dimension. The first subfigure is the real data of the camera man. And the following three subfigures are the outputs of DNNs at step 80, 2000, 58000.]]

In two-dimensional problems, Fig.2 utilises DNN to fit an image of the camera man. The DNN starts learning from a coarse image and produces a more detailed image as training progresses. This demonstrates learning from low to high frequencies, which is analogous to how the biological brain remembers an image. This example shows the 2D frequency principle, which utilises DNNs for image restoration by leveraging preferences for low frequencies, such as in [[inpainting]] tasks. However, it is important to account for insufficient learning of high-frequency structures. To address this limitation, certain algorithms have been developed, which are introduced in the Applications section.

In high-dimensional problems, one can use projection method to visualize the frequency convergence in one particular direction or use a [[Gaussian filter]] to roughly see the convergence of the low-frequency part and the high-frequency part.<ref name="ofp" />

===Theoretical results===

Based on the following assumptions, i.e., i) certain regularity of target function, sample distribution function and activation function;   ii) bounded training trajectory with loss convergence, Luo et al.<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.4208/csiam-am.SO-2020-0005| issn = 2708-0560| volume = 2| issue = 3| pages = 484–507| last1 = Luo| first1 = Tao| last2 = Ma| first2 = Zheng| last3 = Xu| first3 = Zhi-Qin John| last4 = Zhang| first4 = Yaoyu| title = Theory of the Frequency Principle for General Deep Neural Networks| journal = CSIAM Transactions on Applied Mathematics| accessdate = 2023-07-14| date = 2021| s2cid = 195317121| url = http://global-sci.org/intro/article_detail/csiam-am/19447.html| arxiv = 1906.09235}}</ref> proved that the change of high-frequency loss over the total loss decays with the separated frequency with a certain power, which is determined by the regularity assumption. A key aspect of the proof is that composite functions maintain a certain regularity, causing decay in the frequency domain. Thus this result can be applied to general network structures with multiple layers. While this characterization of the F-Principle is very general, it is too coarse-grained to differentiate the effects of network structure or special properties of DNNs. It provides only a qualitative understanding rather than quantitatively characterizing differences.

There is a continuous framework<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1007/s11425-020-1773-8| issn = 1869-1862| volume = 63| issue = 11| pages = 2233–2266| last1 = E| first1 = Weinan| last2 = Ma| first2 = Chao| last3 = Wu| first3 = Lei| title = Machine learning from a continuous viewpoint, I| journal = Science China Mathematics| accessdate = 2023-07-14| date = 2020-11-01| arxiv = 1912.12777| s2cid = 209515941| url = https://doi.org/10.1007/s11425-020-1773-8}}</ref> to study machine learning and suggest gradient flows of neural networks are nice flows and obey the F-Principle. This is because they are [[integral equation]]s which have higher regularity. The increased regularity of integral equations leads to faster decay in the Fourier domain.

==Applications==
===Algorithms designed to overcome the challenge of high-frequency===
'''Phase shift DNN:''' PhaseDNN<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1137/19M1310050| issn = 1064-8275| volume = 42| issue = 5| pages = –3285–A3312| last1 = Cai| first1 = Wei| last2 = Li| first2 = Xiaoguang| last3 = Liu| first3 = Lizuo| title = A Phase Shift Deep Neural Network for High Frequency Approximation and Wave Problems| journal = SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing| accessdate = 2023-07-16| date = 2020| arxiv = 1909.11759| bibcode = 2020SJSC...42A3285C| s2cid = 209376162| url = https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/19M1310050}}</ref> converts high-frequency component of the data downward to a low-frequency spectrum for learning, and then converts the learned one back to the original high frequency.

'''Adaptive activation functions:''' Adaptive activation functions<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/j.jcp.2019.109136| issn = 0021-9991| volume = 404| article-number = 109136| last1 = Jagtap| first1 = Ameya D.| last2 = Kawaguchi| first2 = Kenji| last3 = Karniadakis| first3 = George Em| title = Adaptive activation functions accelerate convergence in deep and physics-informed neural networks| journal = Journal of Computational Physics| accessdate = 2023-07-16| date = 2020-03-01| arxiv = 1906.01170| bibcode = 2020JCoPh.40409136J| s2cid = 174797885| url = https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021999119308411}}</ref> replace the activation function <math>\sigma(x)</math>   by <math>\sigma(\mu ax)</math>, where <math>\mu</math> is a fixed scale factor with  <math>\mu\geq1</math> and <math>a</math> is a trainable variable shared for all neurons.

[[File:MscaleDNN.png|thumb|Fig 3: Illustration of two MscaleDNN structures.]]
'''Multi-scale DNN:''' To alleviate the high-frequency difficulty for high-dimensional problems, a Multi-scale DNN (MscaleDNN) method<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.4208/cicp.OA-2020-0179| issn = 1815-2406| volume = 28| issue = 5| pages = 1970–2001| last1 = Liu| first1 = Ziqi| last2 = Cai| first2 = Wei| last3=Xu| first3 = Zhi-Qin John| title = Multi-Scale Deep Neural Network (MscaleDNN) for Solving Poisson-Boltzmann Equation in Complex Domains| journal = Communications in Computational Physics| accessdate = 2023-07-16| date = 2020| arxiv = 2007.11207| bibcode = 2020CCoPh..28.1970L| s2cid = 220686331| url = http://global-sci.org/intro/article_detail/cicp/18402.html}}</ref> considers the frequency conversion only in the radial direction. The conversion in the frequency space can be done by scaling, which is equivalent to an inverse scaling in the spatial space.

For the first a MscaleDNN takes the following form <math>
    f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \boldsymbol{W}^{[L-1]} \sigma\circ(\cdots (\boldsymbol{W}^{[1]} \sigma\circ(\boldsymbol{K}\odot(\boldsymbol{W}^{[0]} \boldsymbol{x}) + \boldsymbol{b}^{[0]} ) + \boldsymbol{b}^{[1]} )\cdots)+\boldsymbol{b}^{[L-1]}, 
</math>
where <math>\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d</math>, <math>\boldsymbol{W}^{[l]}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{l+1}\times m_{l}}</math>, <math>m_l</math> is the neuron number of <math>l</math>-th hidden layer, <math>m_0=d</math>, <math>\boldsymbol{b}^{[l]}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{l+1}}</math>,
<math>\sigma</math> is a scalar function and <math>\circ</math> means entry-wise operation, <math>\odot</math> is the Hadamard product and<math>\boldsymbol{K}=(\underbrace{a_1,a_1,\cdots,a_1}_{\text{1st part}},a_2,\cdots,a_{i-1},\underbrace{a_i,a_i,\cdots,a_i}_{\text{ith part}},\cdots,\underbrace{a_{N},a_{N}\cdots,a_{N}}_{\text{Nth part}})^T</math> where <math>\boldsymbol{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}}</math>, <math>a_i=i</math> or <math>a_i=2^{i-1}</math>. This structure is called Multi-scale DNN-1 (MscaleDNN-1).

The second kind of MscaleDNN which is denoted as MscaleDNN-2 in Fig.3 is a sum of <math>N</math> subnetworks, in which each scale input goes through a subnetwork.  In MscaleDNN-2, weight matrices from <math>W^{[1]}</math> to <math>W^{[L-1]}</math> are block diagonal. Again, the scale coefficient <math>a_i=i</math> or <math>a_i=2^{i-1}</math>.

'''Fourier feature network:''' Fourier feature network<ref>{{cite arXiv| eprint = 2006.10739| last1 = Tancik| first1 = Matthew| last2 = Srinivasan| first2 = Pratul P.| last3 = Mildenhall| first3 = Ben| last4 = Fridovich-Keil| first4 = Sara| last5 = Raghavan| first5 = Nithin| last6 = Singhal| first6 = Utkarsh| last7 = Ramamoorthi| first7 = Ravi| last8 = Barron| first8 = Jonathan T.| last9 = Ng| first9 = Ren| title = Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency Functions in Low Dimensional Domains| date = 2020-06-18| class = cs.CV}}</ref> map input <math>\boldsymbol{x}</math> to <math>\gamma(\boldsymbol{x})=[a_1 \cos(2\pi \boldsymbol{b}_{1}^{T}\boldsymbol{x}), a_1 \cos(2\pi \boldsymbol{b}_{1}^{T}\boldsymbol{x}),\cdots ,a_m \cos(2\pi \boldsymbol{b}_{m}^{T}\boldsymbol{x}),a_m \cos(2\pi \boldsymbol{b}_{m}^{T}\boldsymbol{x})]</math> for imaging reconstruction tasks. <math>\gamma(\boldsymbol{x})</math> is then used as the input to neural network. An extended Fourier feature network<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/j.cma.2021.113938| issn = 0045-7825| volume = 384| article-number = 113938| last1 = Wang| first1 = Sifan| last2 = Wang| first2 = Hanwen| last3 = Perdikaris| first3 = Paris| title = On the eigenvector bias of Fourier feature networks: From regression to solving multi-scale PDEs with physics-informed neural networks| journal = Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering| accessdate = 2023-07-17| date = 2021-10-01| arxiv = 2012.10047| bibcode = 2021CMAME.384k3938W| s2cid = 229331851| url = https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045782521002759}}</ref> for PDE problem, where the selection for <math>b_i</math> is from different ranges. Ben Mildenhall et al. successfully apply this multiscale Fourier feature input in the neural radiance fields for [[view synthesis]].<ref>{{cite arXiv| eprint = 2003.08934| last1 = Mildenhall| first1 = Ben| last2 = Srinivasan| first2 = Pratul P.| last3 = Tancik| first3 = Matthew| last4 = Barron| first4 = Jonathan T.| last5 = Ramamoorthi| first5 = Ravi| last6 = Ng| first6 = Ren| title = NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis| date = 2020-08-03| class = cs.CV}}</ref>

'''Multi-stage neural network:''' Multi-stage neural networks (MSNN)<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Yongji |last2=Lai |first2=Ching-Yao |title=Multi-stage neural networks: Function approximator of machine precision |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |date=1 May 2024 |volume=504 |article-number=112865 |doi=10.1016/j.jcp.2024.112865 |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2024.112865 |issn=0021-9991|arxiv=2307.08934 |bibcode=2024JCoPh.50412865W }}</ref> use a superposition of DNNs, where sequential neural networks are optimized to fit the residuals from previous neural networks, boosting approximation accuracy. MSNNs have been applied to both regression problems and [[physics-informed neural networks]], effectively addressing spectral bias and achieving accuracy close to the machine precision of double-floating point.

===Frequency perspective for understanding experimental phenomena===
'''Compression phase:''' The F-Principle explains the compression phase in information plane.<ref>{{cite arXiv| eprint = 1703.00810| last1 = Shwartz-Ziv| first1 = Ravid| last2 = Tishby| first2 = Naftali| title = Opening the Black Box of Deep Neural Networks via Information| date = 2017-04-29| class = cs.LG}}</ref><ref name="ipsum"/> The entropy or information quantifies the possibility of output values, i.e., more possible output values lead to a higher entropy. In learning a discretized function, the DNN first fits
the continuous low-frequency components of the discretized function, i.e., large entropy state. Then, the DNN output tends to be discretized as the network gradually captures the high-frequency components, i.e., entropy decreasing. Thus, the compression phase appears in the information plane.

'''Increasing complexity:''' The F-Principle also explains the increasing complexity of DNN output during the training.

'''Strength and limitation:''' The F-Principle points out that deep neural networks are good at learning low-frequency functions but difficult to learn high-frequency functions.

''' [[Early stopping|Early-stopping]] trick:''' As noise is often dominated by high-frequencies, with early-stopping, a neural network with spectral bias can avoid learning high-frequency noise.
